**Rust** is a [general-purpose programming language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General-purpose_programming_language) that emphasizes [performance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_performance), [type safety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Type_safety), [concurrency](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concurrency_(computer_science)>), and [memory safety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memory_safety). Rust supports multiple [programming paradigms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Programming_paradigm). It was influenced by ideas from [functional programming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Functional_programming), including [immutability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immutability), [higher-order functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Higher-order_function), [algebraic data types](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_data_type), and [pattern matching](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pattern_matching). Rust also provides structs, [enums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_type), traits, and methods as alternatives to traditional [object-oriented programming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Object-oriented_programming), without relying on classes or inheritance. Rust enforces memory safety (i.e., that all [references](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reference_(computer_science)>) point to valid memory) without a conventional [garbage collector](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garbage_collection_(computer_science)>); instead, memory safety errors and [data races](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_race) are prevented by the *borrow checker*, which tracks the [object lifetime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Object_lifetime) of references at [compile time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compile_time).

Software developer Graydon Hoare created Rust in 2006 while working at [Mozilla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mozilla), which officially sponsored the project in 2009. The first stable release, Rust 1.0, was published in May 2015. The project has been sponsored by the [Rust Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org#Rust_Foundation) since February 2021. Rust has been adopted by software projects, especially in [web services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Web_service) and [system software](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/System_software). It has been studied academically and has a community of developers.

In 2006, Rust began as a personal project by [Mozilla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mozilla) employee Graydon Hoare. According to *[MIT Technology Review](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MIT_Technology_Review)*, he started the project due to his frustration with a broken elevator in his apartment building whose software had crashed,<sup>[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-MITTechReview-25)</sup> and named the language after the [fungi of the same name](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rust_(fungus)>) that are "over-engineered for survival".<sup>[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-MITTechReview-25)</sup> Between 2006 and 2009, Rust was not publicized to others at Mozilla and was written in Hoare's free time.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-Klabnik2016ACMHistory-26)<sup>: 7:50</sup>  Hoare began speaking about the language around 2009 after a small group at Mozilla became interested.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-Hoare2010-27)

Early contributors have agreed that the language was based primarily on existing ideas. Hoare cited languages from the 1970s, 1980s, and 1990s as influences — including [CLU](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CLU_(programming_language)>), [BETA](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BETA_(programming_language)>), [Mesa](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesa_(programming_language)>), NIL,[\[note 4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-nil-11)[Erlang](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erlang_(programming_language)>), [Newsqueak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newsqueak), [Napier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Napier88), [Hermes](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermes_(programming_language)>), [Sather](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sather), [Alef](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alef_(programming_language)>), and [Limbo](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limbo_(programming_language)>).<sup>[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-Hoare2010-27)</sup> He described the language as "technology from the past come to save the future from itself."[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-Klabnik2016ACMHistory-26)<sup>: 8:17</sup> <sup>[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-Hoare2010-27)</sup> Early contributor Manish Goregaokar similarly described it as based on "mostly decades-old research."[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-MITTechReview-25)

The first [compiler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compiler) was written in about 38,000 lines of [OCaml](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OCaml).[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-Klabnik2016ACMHistory-26)<sup>: 15:34</sup> <sup>[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-OCamlCompiler-28)</sup> It supported a number of features no longer present today, including explicit [object-oriented programming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Object-oriented_programming) via an `obj` keyword[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-Klabnik2016ACMHistory-26)<sup>: 10:08</sup>  and a [typestate analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Typestate_analysis) system tracking variable state such as going from uninitialized to initialized.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-Klabnik2016ACMHistory-26)<sup>: 13:12</sup> 

In 2009, Mozilla officially sponsored the project.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-MITTechReview-25)[Brendan Eich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brendan_Eich) and other executives, intrigued by the possibility of using Rust for a safe [web browser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Web_browser) engine, placed engineers on the project including, Patrick Walton, Niko Matsakis, Felix Klock, and Manish Goregaokar.<sup>[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-MITTechReview-25)</sup> A conference room taken by the project developers was dubbed "the nerd cave", with a sign placed outside the door.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-MITTechReview-25)

Work shifted from the OCaml compiler to a [self-hosting compiler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-hosting_compiler) (*i.e.*, written in Rust) targeting [LLVM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LLVM).[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-Rust0.1-29)<sup>[\[note 5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-31)</sup> The ownership system was in place by 2010.<sup>[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-MITTechReview-25)</sup> The Rust logo was developed in 2011 based on a bicycle [chainring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chainring).<sup>[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-32)</sup> The early 2010s witnessed increasing involvement from full-time engineers at Mozilla and open-source contributors.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-MITTechReview-25)

On January 20, 2012, Rust 0.1 became the first public release<sup>[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-Rust0.1a-1)</sup> for Windows, Linux, and macOS.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-ExtremeTechRust0.1-33)

The following years were marked by substantial changes to the Rust [type system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Type_system).[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-Klabnik2016ACMHistory-26)<sup>: 18:36</sup> <sup>[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-MITTechReview-25)</sup> Memory management through the ownership system was gradually consolidated and expanded; by 2013, the [garbage collector](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garbage_collection_(computer_science)>) was rarely used and was removed.<sup>[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-MITTechReview-25)</sup> Also removed were typestates, the `pure` keyword,<sup>[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-34)</sup> various specialized pointer types, and syntax support for [channels](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Channel_(programming)>).[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-Klabnik2016ACMHistory-26)<sup>: 22:32</sup> 

According to Steve Klabnik, the language was influenced during this period by developers coming from [C++](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C++) (e.g., low-level performance of features), [scripting languages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scripting_language) (e.g., Cargo and package management), and [functional programming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Functional_programming) (e.g., the type system).[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-Klabnik2016ACMHistory-26)<sup>: 30:50</sup> 

In 2013, Graydon Hoare stepped down from Rust.<sup>[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-MITTechReview-25)</sup> After Hoare's departure, Rust evolved organically under a federated governance structure, with a "core team" of initially six people,[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-Klabnik2016ACMHistory-26)<sup>: 21:45</sup>  and around 30–40 developers total across various other teams.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-Klabnik2016ACMHistory-26)<sup>: 22:22</sup>  In March 2014, a [Request for Comments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Request_for_Comments) (RFC) process for new language features was added.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-Klabnik2016ACMHistory-26)<sup>: 33:47</sup>  In 2016, the core team comprised nine people[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-Klabnik2016ACMHistory-26)<sup>: 21:45</sup>  and there were over 1,600 RFCs.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-Klabnik2016ACMHistory-26)<sup>: 34:08</sup> 

Development focused on finalizing features for version 1.0 (which would begin providing [backward compatibility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Backward_compatibility)).[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-Klabnik2016ACMHistory-26)<sup>: 41:26</sup>  According to Andrew Binstock writing for *[Dr. Dobb's Journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dr._Dobb's_Journal)* in January 2014, while Rust was "widely viewed as a remarkably elegant language", adoption slowed because it radically changed from version to version.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-35)

On May 15, 2015, Rust 1.0 became the first [stable release](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stable_release).<sup>[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-MITTechReview-25)</sup> One year later, the compiler had accumulated at least 1,400 contributors, and there were at least 5,000 third-party libraries published on the package-management website Crates.io.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-Klabnik2016ACMHistory-26)<sup>: 43:15</sup> 

The development of the [Servo browser engine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Servo_browser_engine) continued in parallel with Rust, funded by Mozilla and [Samsung](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samsung).<sup>[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-36)</sup> New features in Rust were tested out by the Servo team, and new features in Servo were used to give feedback to the Rust team.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-Klabnik2016ACMHistory-26)<sup>: 5:41</sup>  The first version of Servo was released in 2016.<sup>[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-MITTechReview-25)</sup> The [Firefox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Firefox) web browser shipped with Rust code in 2016 (version 45),[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-Klabnik2016ACMHistory-26)<sup>: 53:30</sup> <sup>[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-37)</sup> but components of Servo did not appear in Firefox until September 2017 (version 57) as part of the [Gecko](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gecko_(software)>) and [Quantum](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gecko_(software)#Quantum>) projects.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-38)

In the years following 1.0, improvements were made to the toolchain ecosystem including [Rustfmt](https://en.wikipedia.org#Rustfmt), [integrated development environment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integrated_development_environment) (IDE) support,[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-Klabnik2016ACMHistory-26)<sup>: 44:56</sup>  and a regular compiler testing and release cycle.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-Klabnik2016ACMHistory-26)<sup>: 46:48</sup>  Rust's community gained a [code of conduct](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Code_of_conduct) and an [IRC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IRC) chat for discussion.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-Klabnik2016ACMHistory-26)<sup>: 50:36</sup> 

The earliest known adoption outside of Mozilla was by individual projects at Samsung, [Facebook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Facebook) (now [Meta Platforms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meta_Platforms)), [Dropbox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropbox), and Tilde, Inc., the company behind [Ember.js](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ember.js).[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-Klabnik2016ACMHistory-26)<sup>: 55:44</sup> [\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-MITTechReview-25)[Amazon Web Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_Web_Services) followed in 2020.<sup>[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-MITTechReview-25)</sup> Engineers cited performance, lack of a garbage collector, safety, and developer experience as reasons for the adoption. Amazon developers cited a 2017 research finding that Rust code was more [energy efficient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Energy_efficiency_in_computing) compared to similar [Java](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Java_(programming_language)>) code.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-MITTechReview-25)[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-2017PortugalEnergyStudy-39)

In August 2020, Mozilla laid off 250 of its 1,000 employees as part of a corporate restructuring during the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic).[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-40)<sup>[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-41)</sup> The Servo team was disbanded. The event raised concerns about the future of Rust.<sup>[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-42)</sup> The Rust Core Team acknowledged the impact of the layoffs and announced plans for an independent foundation. Its first goal would be to own and take financial responsibility for [trademarks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trademark) and [domain names](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domain_name).[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-43)

On February 8, 2021, the [Rust Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org#Rust_Foundation) was formed by founding companies [Amazon Web Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_Web_Services), [Google](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Google), [Huawei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huawei), [Microsoft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microsoft), and [Mozilla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mozilla).[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-44)<sup>[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-45)</sup> The foundation would support developers financially through grants and server funding.<sup>[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-MITTechReview-25)</sup> In an April 6, 2021, blog post, Google announced support for Rust within the [Android Open Source Project](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Android_Open_Source_Project).<sup>[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-46)</sup> Facebook ([Meta Platforms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meta_Platforms)) joined the foundation in April 2021,<sup>[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-47)</sup> followed by ARM ([Arm Holdings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arm_Holdings)) in November.[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-48)

On November 22, 2021, the Moderation Team, responsible for enforcing the community code of conduct, resigned "in protest of the Core Team placing themselves unaccountable to anyone but themselves".<sup>[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-moderation-49)</sup> In May 2022, members of the Rust leadership council published a response to the incident.[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-50)

On April 6, 2023, the Rust Foundation posted a draft for a new trademark policy that resulted in widespread negative reactions.<sup>[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-ApologizesTrademarkPolicy-51)</sup> The trademark policy included rules for how the Rust logo and name could be used.[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-ApologizesTrademarkPolicy-51)

Rust's [syntax](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syntax_(programming_languages)>) is similar to that of [C](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C_(programming_language)>) and [C++](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C++),[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-53)<sup>[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-:4-54)</sup> although many of its features were influenced by [functional programming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Functional_programming) languages such as [OCaml](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OCaml).<sup>[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols2019263-55)</sup> Hoare has described Rust as targeted at frustrated C++ developers.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-Hoare2010-27)

Below is a ["Hello, World!" program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/"Hello,_World!"_program) in Rust. The `fn` keyword denotes a [function](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Function_(computer_programming)>), and the `println!` [macro](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macro_(computer_science)>) (see [§ Macros](https://en.wikipedia.org#Macros)) prints the message to [standard output](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_output).[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols20195–6-56)[Statements](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statement_(computer_science)>) in Rust are separated by [semicolons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semicolon#Programming).

```
fn main() {
    println!("Hello, World!");
}
```
[Variables](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variable_(computer_science)>) in Rust are defined through the `let` keyword.<sup>[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols202332-57)</sup> The example below assigns a value to the variable with name `foo` of type `i32` and outputs its value; the type annotation `: i32` can be omitted.

```
fn main() {
    let foo: i32 = 10;
    println!("The value of foo is {foo}");
}
```
Variables are [immutable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immutable) by default, unless the `mut` keyword is added.<sup>[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols202332–33-58)</sup> The following example uses `//`, which denotes the start of a [comment](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comment_(computer_programming)>).[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols202349–50-59)

```
fn main() {
    // This code would not compile without adding "mut".
    let mut foo = 10;
    println!("The value of foo is {foo}");
    foo = 20;
    println!("The value of foo is {foo}");
}
```
Multiple `let` expressions can define multiple variables with the same name, known as [variable shadowing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variable_shadowing). Variable shadowing allows transforming variables without having to name the variables differently.<sup>[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols202334–36-60)</sup> The example below declares a new variable with the same name that is double the original value:

```
fn main() {
    let foo = 10;
    // This will output "The value of foo is 10"
    println!("The value of foo is {foo}");
    let foo = foo * 2;
    // This will output "The value of foo is 20"
    println!("The value of foo is {foo}");
}
```
Variable shadowing is also possible for values of different types. For example, going from a string to its length:

```
fn main() {
    let letters = "abc";
    let letters = letters.len();
}
```
A *block expression* is delimited by [curly brackets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bracket#Curly_brackets). When the last expression inside a block does not end with a semicolon, the block evaluates to the value of that trailing expression:[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols20236,_47,_53-61)

```
fn main() {
    let x = {
        println!("this is inside the block");
        1 + 2
    };
    println!("1 + 2 = {x}");
}
```
Trailing expressions of function bodies are used as the return value:[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols202347–48-62)

```
fn add_two(x: i32) -> i32 {
    x + 2
}
```
An `if` [conditional expression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conditional_expression) executes code based on whether the given value is `true`. `else` can be used for when the value evaluates to `false`, and `else if` can be used for combining multiple expressions.[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols202350–53-63)

```
fn main() {
    let x = 10;
    if x > 5 {
        println!("value is greater than five");
    }
    if x % 7 == 0 {
        println!("value is divisible by 7");
    } else if x % 5 == 0 {
        println!("value is divisible by 5");
    } else {
        println!("value is not divisible by 7 or 5");
    }
}
```
`if` and `else` blocks can evaluate to a value, which can then be assigned to a variable:[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols202350–53-63)

```
fn main() {
    let x = 10;
    let new_x = if x % 2 == 0 { x / 2 } else { 3 * x + 1 };
    println!("{new_x}");
}
```
[while](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/While_loop)[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols202356-64)

```
fn main() {
    // Iterate over all integers from 4 to 10
    let mut value = 4;
    while value <= 10 {
         println!("value = {value}");
         value += 1;
    }
}
```
[For loops](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/For_loop) in Rust loop over elements of a collection.[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols202357–58-65)`for` expressions work over any [iterator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iterator) type.

```
fn main() {
    // Using `for` with range syntax for the same functionality as above
    // The syntax 4..=10 means the range from 4 to 10, up to and including 10.
    for value in 4..=10 {
        println!("value = {value}");
    }
}
```
In the above code, `4..=10` is a value of type `Range` that implements the `Iterator` trait. The code within the curly braces is applied to each element returned by the iterator.

Iterators can combine with functions over iterators like `map`, `filter`, and `sum`. For example, the following adds up all numbers between 1 and 100 that are multiples of 3:

```
(1..=100).filter(|x| x % 3 == 0).sum()
```
More generally, the `loop` keyword allows repeating a portion of code until a `break` occurs. `break` may optionally exit the loop with a value. In the case of nested loops, labels denoted by `'label_name` can be used to break an outer loop rather than the innermost loop.[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols202354–56-66)

```
fn main() {
    let value = 456;
    let mut x = 1;
    let y = loop {
        x *= 10;
        if x > value {
            break x / 10;
        }
    };
    println!("largest power of ten that is smaller than or equal to value: {y}");
    let mut up = 1;
    'outer: loop {
        let mut down = 120;
        loop {
            if up > 100 {
                break 'outer;
            }
            if down < 4 {
                break;
            }
            down /= 2;
            up += 1;
            println!("up: {up}, down: {down}");
        }
        up *= 2;
    }
}
```
The `match` and `if let` expressions provide [pattern matching](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pattern_matching). For example, `match` can double an optional integer value if present, and return zero otherwise:[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols2019104–109-67)

```
fn double(x: Option<u64>) -> u64 {
    match x {
        Some(value) => value * 2,
        None => 0,
    }
}
```
Equivalently, this can be written with `if let` and `else`:

```
fn double(x: Option<u64>) -> u64 {
    if let Some(value) = x {
        value * 2
    } else {
        0
    }
}
```
Rust is [strongly typed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strongly_typed) and [statically typed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statically_typed), meaning that the types of all variables must be known at compilation time. Assigning a value of a particular type to a differently typed variable causes a [compilation error](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compilation_error). [Type inference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Type_inference) determines the type of variables if unspecified.[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols201924-68)

The [unit type](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unit_type), notated `()` in Rust, is a concrete type that has exactly one value. It occupies no memory (as it represents the absence of value). All functions that do not have an indicated return type implicitly return `()`. It is similar to `void` in other C-style languages; however, `void` denotes the absence of a type and cannot have any value.

The default integer type is `i32`, and the default [floating point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Floating_point) type is `f64`. If the type of a [literal](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literal_(computer_programming)>) number is not explicitly provided, it is either inferred from the context or the default type is used.[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols201936–38-69)

[Integer types](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integer_type) in Rust are named based on the [signedness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Signedness) and the number of bits the type takes. For example, `i32` is a signed integer that takes 32 bits of storage, whereas `u8` is unsigned and only takes 8 bits of storage. `isize` and `usize` take storage depending on the [memory address bus width](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bus_(computing)#Address_bus>) of the compilation target. For example, when building for [32-bit targets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/32-bit_computing), both types will take up 32 bits of space.[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-70)[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-71)

By default, integer literals are in base-10, but different [radices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radix) are supported with prefixes, for example, `0b11` for [binary numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_number), `0o567` for [octals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Octal), and `0xDB` for [hexadecimals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hexadecimal). By default, integer literals default to `i32` as its type. Suffixes such as `4u32` explicitly set the type of a literal.<sup>[\[67\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols202336–38-72)</sup> Byte literals such as `b'X'` are available to represent the [ASCII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ASCII) value (as a `u8`) of a specific character.[\[68\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols2023502-73)

The [Boolean type](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boolean_type) is referred to as `bool`, which takes a value of either `true` or `false`. A `char` takes up 32 bits of space and represents a Unicode scalar value:<sup>[\[69\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-74)</sup> a [Unicode codepoint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unicode_codepoint) that is not a [surrogate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Character_Set_characters#Surrogates).[\[70\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-75)[IEEE 754](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IEEE_754) floating point numbers are supported with `f32` for [single precision floats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single_precision_float) and `f64` for [double precision floats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_precision_float).[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols201938–40-76)

Compound types can contain multiple values. Tuples are fixed-size lists that contain values whose types can be different. Arrays are fixed-size lists whose values are of the same type. Expressions of the tuple and array types are written through listing the values, and can be accessed with `.index` (with tuples) or `[index]` (with arrays):[\[72\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols202340–42-77)

```
let tuple: (u32, bool) = (3, true);
let array: [i8; 5] = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];
let value = tuple.1; // true
let value = array[2]; // 3
```
Arrays can also be constructed through copying a single value a number of times:[\[73\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols202342-78)

```
let array2: [char; 10] = [' '; 10];
```
Rust's ownership system consists of rules that ensure memory safety without using a garbage collector. At compile time, each value must be attached to a variable called the *owner* of that value, and every value must have exactly one owner.<sup>[\[74\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols201959–61-79)</sup> Values are moved between different owners through assignment or passing a value as a function parameter. Values can also be *borrowed,*—temporarily passed to a different function before being returned to the owner.<sup>[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols201963–68-80)</sup> With these rules, Rust prevents creation and use of [dangling pointers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dangling_pointers):[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols201963–68-80)[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols201974–75-81)

```
fn print_string(s: String) {
    println!("{}", s);
}
fn main() {
    let s = String::from("Hello, World");
    print_string(s); // s consumed by print_string
    // s has been moved, so cannot be used any more
    // another print_string(s); would result in a compile error
}
```
The function `print_string` takes ownership over the `String` value passed in; Alternatively, `&` can be used to indicate a [reference](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reference_(computer_science)>) type (in `&String`) and to create a reference (in `&s`):[\[77\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols202371–72-82)

```
fn print_string(s: &String) {
    println!("{}", s);
}
fn main() {
    let s = String::from("Hello, World");
    print_string(&s); // s borrowed by print_string
    print_string(&s); // s has not been consumed; we can call the function many times
}
```
Because of these ownership rules, Rust types are known as *[affine types](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affine_type)*, meaning each value may be used at most once. This enforces a form of [software fault isolation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Software_fault_isolation) as the owner of a value is solely responsible for its correctness and deallocation.[\[78\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-BeyondSafety-83)

When a value goes out of scope, it is *dropped* by running its [destructor](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Destructor_(computer_programming)>). The destructor may be programmatically defined through implementing the `Drop` [trait](https://en.wikipedia.org#Traits). This helps manage resources such as file handles, network sockets, and [locks](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lock_(computer_science)>), since when objects are dropped, the resources associated with them are closed or released automatically.[\[79\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols2023327–30-84)

[Object lifetime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Object_lifetime) refers to the period of time that a reference is valid—that is, the time between object creation and destruction.<sup>[\[80\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-85)</sup> These *lifetimes* are implicitly associated with all Rust reference types. While often inferred, they can also be indicated explicitly with named lifetime parameters (often denoted `'a`, `'b`, and so on).[\[81\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-86)

A value's lifetime in Rust is inferred from the set of locations in the source code (i.e., function, line, and column numbers) for which a variable is valid.<sup>[\[82\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols2019194-87)</sup> For example, a reference to a local variable has a lifetime from the expression it is declared in up until the last use of it.[\[82\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols2019194-87)

```
fn main() {
    let mut x = 5;            // ------------------+- Lifetime 'a
                              //                   |
    let r = &x;               // -+-- Lifetime 'b  |
                              //  |                |
    println!("r: {}", r);     // -+                |
    // Since r is no longer used,                  |
    // its lifetime ends                           |
    let r2 = &mut x;          // -+-- Lifetime 'c  |
}                             // ------------------+
```
The borrow checker in the Rust compiler then enforces that references are only used in the locations of the source code where the associated lifetime is valid.[\[83\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols201975,_134-88)<sup>[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-89)</sup> In the example above, storing a reference to variable `x` in `r` is valid, as variable `x` has a longer lifetime (`'a`) than variable `r` (`'b`). However, when `x` has a shorter lifetime, the borrow checker would reject the program:

```
fn main() {
    let r;                    // ------------------+- Lifetime 'a
                              //                   |
    {                         //                   |
        let x = 5;            // -+-- Lifetime 'b  |
        r = &x; // ERROR: x does  |                |
    }           // not live long -|                |
                // enough                          |
    println!("r: {}", r);     //                   |
}                             // ------------------+
```
Since the lifetime of the referenced variable (`'b`) is shorter than the lifetime of the variable holding the reference (`'a`), the borrow checker errors, preventing `x` from being used from outside its scope.[\[85\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols2019194–195-90)

Lifetimes can be indicated using explicit *lifetime parameters* on function arguments. For example, the following code specifies that the reference returned by the function has the same lifetime as `original` (and *not* necessarily the same lifetime as `prefix`):[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols2023208–12-91)

```
fn remove_prefix<'a>(mut original: &'a str, prefix: &str) -> &'a str {
    if original.starts_with(prefix) {
        original = original[prefix.len()..];
    }
    original
}
```
In the compiler, ownership and lifetimes work together to prevent memory safety issues such as dangling pointers.[\[87\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols2023[httpsdocrust-langorgbookch04-02-references-and-borrowinghtml_4.2._References_and_Borrowing]-92)[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-Pearce-93)

User-defined types are created with the `struct` or `enum` keywords. The `struct` keyword denotes a [record type](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Record_(computer_science)>) that groups multiple related values.[\[89\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols201983-94)`enum`s can take on different variants at runtime, with their capabilities similar to [algebraic data types](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_data_types) found in functional programming languages.<sup>[\[90\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols201997-95)</sup> Both records and enum variants can contain [fields](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_(computer_science)>) with different types.<sup>[\[91\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols201998–101-96)</sup> Alternative names, or aliases, for the same type can be defined with the `type` keyword.[\[92\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols2019438–440-97)

The `impl` keyword can define methods for a user-defined type. Data and functions are defined separately. Implementations fulfill a role similar to that of [classes](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Class_(programming)>) within other languages.[\[93\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols201993-98)

The Rust [standard library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_library) defines and implements many widely used custom data types, including core data structures such as `Vec`, `Option`, and `HashMap`, as well as [smart pointer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smart_pointer) types. Rust provides a way to exclude most of the standard library using the attribute `#![no_std]`, for applications such as embedded devices. Internally, the standard library is divided into three parts, `core`, `alloc`, and `std`, where `std` and `alloc` are excluded by `#![no_std]`.[\[94\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGjengset2021213–215-99)

Rust uses the [option type](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Option_type) `Option<T>` to define optional values, which can be matched using `if let` or `match` to access the inner value:[\[95\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols2023108–110,_113–114,_116–117-100)

```
fn main() {
    let name1: Option<&str> = None;
    // In this case, nothing will be printed out
    if let Some(name) = name1 {
        println!("{name}");
    }
    let name2: Option<&str> = Some("Matthew");
    // In this case, the word "Matthew" will be printed out
    if let Some(name) = name2 {
        println!("{name}");
    }
}
```
Similarly, Rust's [result type](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Result_type) `Result<T, E>` holds either a successfully computed value (the `Ok` variant) or an error (the `Err` variant).<sup>[\[96\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-Rust_error_handling-101)</sup> Like `Option`, the use of `Result` means that the inner value cannot be used directly; programmers must use a `match` expression, syntactic sugar such as `?` (the "try" operator), or an explicit `unwrap` assertion to access it. Both `Option` and `Result` are used throughout the standard library and are a fundamental part of Rust's explicit approach to handling errors and missing data.

The `&` and `&mut` reference types are guaranteed to not be null and point to valid memory.<sup>[\[97\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGjengset2021155-156-102)</sup> The raw pointer types `*const` and `*mut` opt out of the safety guarantees, thus they may be null or invalid; however, it is impossible to dereference them unless the code is explicitly declared unsafe through the use of an `unsafe` block.<sup>[\[98\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols2023421–423-103)</sup> Unlike dereferencing, the creation of raw pointers is allowed inside safe Rust code.[\[99\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols2019418–427-104)

Rust provides no implicit type conversion (coercion) between most primitive types. But, explicit type conversion (casting) can be performed using the `as` keyword.[\[100\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-105)

```
let x: i32 = 1000;
println!("1000 as a u16 is: {}", x as u16);
```
Rust supports [polymorphism](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polymorphism_(computer_science)>) through [traits](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trait_(computer_programming)>), [generic functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generic_function), and [trait objects](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trait_object_(Rust)>).[\[101\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols2023378-106)

Common behavior between types is declared using traits and `impl` blocks:[\[102\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols2023192–198-107)

```
trait Zero: Sized {
    fn zero() -> Self;
    fn is_zero(&self) -> bool
    where
        Self: PartialEq,
    {
        self == &Zero::zero()
    }
}
impl Zero for u32 {
    fn zero() -> u32 { 0 }
}
impl Zero for f32 {
    fn zero() -> Self { 0.0 }
}
```
The example above includes a method `is_zero` that provides a default implementation that may be overridden when implementing the trait.[\[102\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols2023192–198-107)

A function can be made generic by adding type parameters inside angle brackets (`<Num>`), which only allow types that implement the trait:

```
// zero is a generic function with one type parameter, Num
fn zero<Num: Zero>() -> Num {
    Num::zero()
}
fn main() {
    let a: u32 = zero();
    let b: f32 = zero();
    assert!(a.is_zero() && b.is_zero());
}
```
In the examples above, `Num: Zero` as well as `where Self: PartialEq` are trait bounds that constrain the type to only allow types that implement `Zero` or `PartialEq`.<sup>[\[102\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols2023192–198-107)</sup> Within a trait or impl, `Self` refers to the type that the code is implementing.[\[103\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols202398-108)

Generics can be used in functions to allow implementing a behavior for different types without repeating the same code (see [bounded parametric polymorphism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bounded_parametric_polymorphism)). Generic functions can be written in relation to other generics, without knowing the actual type.[\[104\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols2019171–172,_205-109)

By default, traits use [static dispatch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Static_dispatch): the compiler [monomorphizes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monomorphization) the function for each concrete type instance, yielding performance equivalent to type-specific code at the cost of longer compile times and larger binaries.[\[105\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols2023191–192-110)

When the exact type is not known at compile time, Rust provides [trait objects](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trait_object_(Rust)>) `&dyn Tr` and `Box<dyn Tr>`, where `Tr` is a trait.<sup>[\[106\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols2019441–442-111)</sup> Trait object calls use [dynamic dispatch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamic_dispatch) via a lookup table; a trait object is a "fat pointer" carrying both a data pointer and a method table pointer.<sup>[\[105\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols2023191–192-110)</sup> This indirection adds a small runtime cost, but it keeps a single copy of the code and reduces binary size. Only "object-safe" traits are eligible to be used as trait objects.[\[107\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGjengset202125-112)

This approach is similar to [duck typing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duck_typing), where all data types that implement a given trait can be treated as functionally interchangeable.<sup>[\[108\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols2023[httpsdocrust-langorgbookch18-02-trait-objectshtml_18.2._Using_Trait_Objects_That_Allow_for_Values_of_Different_Types]-113)</sup> The following example creates a list of objects where each object implements the `Display` trait:

```
use std::fmt::Display;
fn main() {
    let v: Vec<Box<dyn Display>> = vec![
        Box::new(3),
        Box::new(5.0),
        Box::new("hi"),
    ];
    for x in v {
        println!("{x}");
    }
}
```
If an element in the list does not implement the `Display` trait, it will cause a compile-time error.[\[109\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols2019379–380-114)

Rust does not use [garbage collection](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garbage_collection_(computer_science)>). Memory and other resources are instead managed through the "[resource acquisition is initialization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resource_acquisition_is_initialization)" convention,<sup>[\[110\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-115)</sup> with optional [reference counting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reference_counting). Rust provides deterministic management of resources, with very low [overhead](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overhead_(computing)>).<sup>[\[111\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-116)</sup> Values are [allocated on the stack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stack-based_memory_allocation) by default, and all [dynamic allocations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamic_allocation) must be explicit.[\[112\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-117)

The built-in reference types using the `&` symbol do not involve run-time reference counting. The safety and validity of the underlying pointers are verified at compile time, preventing [dangling pointers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dangling_pointers) and other forms of [undefined behavior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Undefined_behavior).<sup>[\[113\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols201970–75-118)</sup> Rust's type system separates shared, [immutable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immutable) references of the form `&T` from unique, mutable references of the form `&mut T`. A mutable reference can be coerced to an immutable reference, but not vice versa.[\[114\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols2019323-119)

Rust's memory safety checks (See [#Safety](https://en.wikipedia.org#Safety)) may be circumvented through the use of `unsafe` blocks. This allows programmers to dereference arbitrary raw pointers, call external code, or perform other low-level functionality not allowed by safe Rust.<sup>[\[115\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols2023420–429-120)</sup> Some low-level functionality enabled in this way includes [volatile memory access](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volatile_(computer_programming)>), architecture-specific intrinsics, [type punning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Type_punning), and inline assembly.[\[116\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcNamara2021139,_376–379,_395-121)

Unsafe code is needed, for example, in the implementation of data structures.<sup>[\[117\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-UnsafeRustUse-122)</sup> A frequently cited example is that it is difficult or impossible to implement [doubly linked lists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doubly_linked_list) in safe Rust.[\[118\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-123)[\[119\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-124)[\[120\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-125)[\[121\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-126)

Programmers using unsafe Rust are considered responsible for upholding Rust's memory and type safety requirements, for example, that no two mutable references exist pointing to the same location.<sup>[\[122\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-IsRustSafely-127)</sup> If programmers write code that violates these requirements, this results in [undefined behavior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Undefined_behavior).<sup>[\[122\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-IsRustSafely-127)</sup> The Rust documentation includes a list of behaviors considered undefined, including accessing dangling or misaligned pointers, or breaking the aliasing rules for references.[\[123\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-128)

Macros allow the generation and transformation of Rust code to reduce repetition. Macros come in two forms, with *declarative macros* defined through `macro_rules!`, and *procedural macros*, which are defined in separate crates.[\[124\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols2023449–455-129)[\[125\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGjengset2021101–102-130)

A declarative macro (also called a "macro by example") is a macro, defined using the `macro_rules!` keyword, that uses pattern matching to determine its expansion.[\[126\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-Rust_Ref._–_Macros_By_Example-131)<sup>[\[127\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols2019446–448-132)</sup> Below is an example that sums over all its arguments:

```
macro_rules! sum {
    ( $initial:expr $(, $expr:expr )* $(,)? ) => {
        $initial $(+ $expr)*
    }
}
fn main() {
    let x = sum!(1, 2, 3);
    println!("{x}"); // prints 6
}
```
In this example, the macro named `sum` is defined using the form `macro_rules! sum {` `(...) => { ... } }`. The first part inside the parentheses of the definition, the macro pattern `( $initial:expr $(, $expr:expr )* $(,)? )` specifies the structure of input it can take. Here, `$initial:expr` represents the first expression, while `$(, $expr:expr )*` means there can be zero or more additional comma-separated expressions after it.
